title: The Takeout Tax: You Have $40 of Food in Your Fridge. You Ordered Delivery Anyway.
editorialNotes: Version-stale: pre-Aug-19 7-slide brief; an 8-slide re-brief exists per COVERAGE.md but is not in briefs/.

Statista/DoorDash aggregate figures (3.4 orders/week, $34 average, $6,000+/year) are survey-aggregate and implausible for an average household; rendered as list items, never hero type. Adi should verify before publishing.
"200+ decisions by 6 PM" has no source in the brief.
The brief's visual note prices the fridge food at $6.30 while copy says $4 in ingredients; copy kept verbatim.

copy.headline: Your fridge had $40 of groceries in it.
The average household orders food delivery 3.4 times per week.
items: Add fees, tips, and service charges - the "nothing to eat" tax is $150-200 per month.
copy.citation: Statista delivery frequency data; DoorDash / Uber Eats annual consumer reports.

copy.headline: Why it happens:
items: By 6 PM, your brain has made 200+ decisions.
The fridge asks you to invent a meal from chaos.
The app shows you pictures. The pictures win. Every time.
This isn't laziness - it's decision fatigue. The app is designed to win.

copy.headline: What's in your fridge right now, when you're about to order: half an onion, a chicken breast, two servings of pasta, wilting spinach, three eggs.
items: That's dinner for two. It costs $4 in ingredients and 20 minutes.
It's about to cost $35 and 40 minutes of waiting.

copy.headline: The invisible food problem: When you open the fridge and see chaos, you see scraps - not meals.
copy.body: The food doesn't announce itself as a complete dinner. It just looks like leftovers. The "nothing to eat" feeling is real. The fridge is failing to communicate - and you pay for that failure.

copy.headline: The math over a year:
items: If 2 of those 3 are "nothing to eat" orders - the fridge had $15-40 of food in it - that's $3,640/year in avoidable spend.
Plus the groceries that then expired and got thrown away anyway.

copy.headline: You don't have a "nothing to eat" problem. You have a "can't see what you have" problem.
copy.ctaLine: fond shows you what's in your fridge and what you can make with it. Link in bio.
